intro: In Act I of Puccini’s La bohème, Mimì comes to her neighbour’s attic to have her candle lit and stays to tell him about her life as an embroiderer whose small room gets the first sun of spring. Claudia Muzio sings “Sì, mi chiamano Mimì”.

sections.label: A · Mimì gives her name
sections.mNote: Short phrases extend into a song about flowers and poetry.

sections.label: A′ · opening phrase recurs
sections.mNote: The opening phrase returns, followed by a skipping accompaniment figure.

sections.label: B · Broad melody towards D major
sections.mNote: A broad melody rises towards D major.

sections.label: Coda · The neighbour apologises
sections.mNote: Free, speech-like delivery above a held chord

cues.title: Mimì’s reply to Rodolfo
cues.text: “Mi chiamano Mimì, ma il mio nome è Lucia” — “They call me Mimì, but my name is Lucia.” Rodolfo has told her he is a poet. Seated in his attic, she replies by describing her own work, embroidering lilies and roses on linen or silk.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I: Mimì’s reply to Rodolfo. Ricordi vocal score, pp. 69–70, marks her opening con semplicità, still seated. Italian text: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . Translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dispute with Leoncavallo
cues.text: According to the story, Puccini chose the subject on the train from Turin back to Milan after the triumph of Manon Lescaut. Ruggero Leoncavallo, already writing his own La bohème, claimed priority. Puccini told the Corriere della Sera: “Let him set it to music, then I will. The public will judge.”
cues.evidence: The train ride, the dispute with Leoncavallo, who was at work on the same subject and claimed priority, and Puccini’s reply to the Corriere della Sera, in the Puccini Museum’s English: https://www.puccinimuseum.org/en/giacomo-puccini/le-opere/la-boheme/ . Puccini began drafting the music in June 1893: the same page; the Giacomo Puccini Catalogue of the Works dates the opera’s composition from March 1893: https://catalog.puccini.it/public/works/la-boheme

cues.title: Mimì’s daily life, Allegretto moderato
cues.text: Mimì repeats her name, then tells how she makes her own lunch, prays and lives alone in a little white room. After the opening phrase returns, the score moves into Allegretto moderato over a skipping accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, pp. 71–72: renewed Mi chiamano Mimì marked Lentamente; Sola mi fo il pranzo da me stessa marked Allegretto moderato, con semplicità. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Turin, 1896
cues.text: At the Teatro Regio in Turin on 1 February 1896, Cesira Ferrani sang the first Mimì under the 28-year-old Toscanini. The critics were divided. One review predicted that La bohème “will not leave a big mark in the history of opera”.
cues.evidence: The Giacomo Puccini Catalogue of the Works lists the first performance on 1 February 1896 at the Teatro Regio, Turin, with Cesira Ferrani as Mimì and Arturo Toscanini conducting (Toscanini was born on 25 March 1867): https://catalog.puccini.it/public/works/la-boheme . The Puccini Museum reports that critics were divided and quotes one review, in its English: https://www.puccinimuseum.org/en/giacomo-puccini/le-opere/la-boheme/

cues.title: Candle and key scene, Act I
cues.text: Mimì’s candle goes out and she drops her key in Rodolfo’s room. He finds it and pockets it without telling her, so the search in the dark goes on. Before she begins this aria, he has held her cold hand and told her about his poems.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I, candle-and-key scene preceding the two arias. https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo

cues.title: “Il primo sole è mio”
cues.text: “Il primo sole è mio” — “The first sunshine is mine.” At the thought of spring, Mimì stands up. The tempo changes to Andante molto sostenuto, and her voice rises above an accompaniment that builds to the climax in D major.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 73: stage direction si alza, Andante molto sostenuto and con grande espansione at the climax. Illica and Giacosa’s Act I text; translation ours. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final section of Mimì’s aria
cues.text: The flowers Mimì embroiders have no scent. Her line drops in volume, and she apologises for disturbing her neighbour so late. Puccini marked the last explanation “senza rigore di tempo, con naturalezza” — “without strict time, naturally” — and the soprano speaks over a held chord.
cues.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 74, final paragraph of Mimì’s aria: the embroidered flowers, her apology and Puccini’s tempo instruction. Translation ours. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Mimì begins her introduction again
transitions.how: The first song about flowers and poetry contracts into a brief exchange with Rodolfo. Mimì then repeats her introduction, marked Lentamente in 2/4. The rising phrase returns with chromatic notes and separated chords underneath, and the soprano has room for pauses between her words.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 71: the renewed Mi chiamano Mimì, Lentamente in 2/4, with altered notes and separated accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

transitions.title: Fermata into Andante molto sostenuto
transitions.to: B · Broad melody towards D major
transitions.how: Mimì’s account of looking over the roofs ends on a fermata. The metre changes to common time, marked Andante molto sostenuto. The new melody begins over G-major harmony, and the bass then moves through E and A to the D-major climax.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, pp. 72–73: fermata, common-time Andante molto sostenuto, G-major opening and the E–A–D bass route to the climax. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

transitions.title: Held D-major chord under Mimì’s close
transitions.from: B · Broad melody towards D major
transitions.how: The earlier flower melody returns at a low dynamic. As Mimì explains that her embroidered flowers have no scent, the accompaniment moves to a sustained D-major chord. She sings her final apology in free time over the held chord, marked senza rigore di tempo, con naturalezza. A brief chord closes her introduction.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi vocal score, p. 74: the quiet melodic recall, sustained D-major chord and freely timed final explanation. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP885138-PMLP50378-puccini_mi_chiamano_mimi_from_la_boheme_ricordi.pdf.pdf

source.title: Puccini, La bohème, Act I, full orchestral score (Ricordi)
source.locator: Ricordi full score, PDF pp. 98–107: rehearsal figures 35–38, from Mimì’s introduction to her freely spoken final apology.

timeline.note: Quiet strings accompany Mimì’s introduction; flute, clarinet and harp add brief answers.
Divided strings accompany the song about flowers; woodwinds, harp and quiet percussion join its longer phrases.
Repeated string chords accompany the shorter phrases, with clarinet, bass clarinet and horns.
A solo viola plays beneath Mimì’s returning introduction; the winds are silent.
A flute plays above sparse string notes and harp chords as Mimì describes life alone.
Flute, clarinet and first violins play the spring melody with Mimì; horns and low strings accompany them.
Flutes, horns and high strings double the broad vocal climax, with trumpets and trombones beneath.
The soprano climbs again, accompanied by upper winds, horn and divided strings.
Soft winds, harp and percussion quieten; muted strings accompany the return to conversation.
The strings hold a chord while Mimì sings her final apology freely, then add a short closing chord.

composer.epithet: He held a theatre audience through a scene of a woman at a window, then brought back a tune it had heard before.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Bazzini and Ponchielli
Giulio Ricordi · Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas, counting Il trittico as three; a Mass, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini began at the organ. His family had supplied Lucca with church musicians for generations, and when his father Michele died in 1864, the five-year-old Giacomo was expected to continue the trade. He studied in the town, played in its churches and completed a Mass in 1880. In 1876, however, he had heard Verdi’s Aida in Pisa, and he turned to the theatre. A scholarship helped him into the Milan Conservatory, where Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli taught him composition. His graduation piece of 1883, Capriccio sinfonico, contains the music that later opened La bohème.

He submitted his first opera, Le Villi, to the Sonzogno competition on the last possible day, 31 December 1883; it did not receive a mention. The librettist Ferdinando Fontana arranged a private hearing at the journalist Marco Sala’s house, with Arrigo Boito among the guests. A subscription paid for a performance at Milan’s Teatro Dal Verme the following May. Giulio Ricordi bought the opera and commissioned another. Edgar, first performed at La Scala in 1889, was a failure that Puccini spent years trying to repair.
